variants.title: Choose the pattern
variants.context: A communication pattern answers four questions: does the sender wait, do one or many consumers receive the work, can the system buffer a burst, and what happens on failure. Request-response for immediate results, a work queue for later work, an event stream for many reactions.
variants.prompt: A checkout page needs the current price before it can render. Which pattern?
optionFeedback: The caller needs an immediate result; downstream latency becomes part of its path.
The user cannot continue without the answer.
No one else needs to react to a price lookup.
variants.hint: Does the sender have to wait?
variants.explanation: Use request-response when the caller needs the result now, and protect it with deadlines.

variants.title: Choose the pattern
variants.context: A communication pattern answers four questions: does the sender wait, do one or many consumers receive the work, can the system buffer a burst, and what happens on failure. Request-response for immediate results, a work queue for later work, an event stream for many reactions.
variants.prompt: Thumbnails must be generated for uploaded photos, but the upload response should not wait for them. Which pattern?
optionFeedback: Work that can finish later is queued; handlers must tolerate retries.
Waiting for thumbnails holds the request open.
Only one worker needs each photo; replay is not the requirement.
variants.hint: Can the work finish later, and how many consumers need it?
variants.explanation: A queue absorbs bursts and lets workers scale independently.

variants.title: Choose the pattern
variants.context: A communication pattern answers four questions: does the sender wait, do one or many consumers receive the work, can the system buffer a burst, and what happens on failure. Request-response for immediate results, a work queue for later work, an event stream for many reactions.
variants.prompt: Inventory, billing, analytics, and notifications each react to OrderCreated. Which pattern?
optionFeedback: Several capabilities react to one fact; replay and fan-out make that flexible.
One queue means one consumer owns each message; the others would miss it.
Synchronous fan-out puts every reaction in the checkout latency budget.
variants.hint: How many consumers need their own copy?
variants.explanation: Use an event stream when several capabilities react to a fact that already happened.

variants.title: Compose the workflow
variants.context: Production systems combine patterns: validate synchronously, commit intent with an outbox in one transaction, process durable work through a queue with bounded retries, then publish business facts to a stream for independent reactions.
variants.prompt: An order is placed. Put the composed pattern in order.

items.text: Validate price, inventory policy, and identity synchronously while the user waits.
Store the order and an outbox event in one database transaction.
Run payment capture, fulfillment, and email through a queue with bounded retries and idempotency keys.
Publish business facts to a stream so analytics and audit react independently.

variants.hint: The smallest immediate decision is synchronous; everything else can follow.
variants.explanation: Sync validation → atomic commit with outbox → durable queue work → event stream. Each step gets the behavior it needs.

variants.title: Compose the workflow
variants.context: Production systems combine patterns: validate synchronously, commit intent with an outbox in one transaction, process durable work through a queue with bounded retries, then publish business facts to a stream for independent reactions.
variants.prompt: A signup flow must send a welcome email and update analytics. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Validate the credentials and create the account while the user waits.
Commit the account and an outbox record together.
Deliver the email via a queue with retries and a dead-letter policy.
Publish AccountCreated for analytics and recommendations.

variants.hint: Do not put the email in the signup latency budget.
variants.explanation: The outbox ties state and communication together; the queue and stream keep reactions out of the request path.

variants.title: Compose the workflow
variants.context: Production systems combine patterns: validate synchronously, commit intent with an outbox in one transaction, process durable work through a queue with bounded retries, then publish business facts to a stream for independent reactions.
variants.prompt: A refund is requested. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Check eligibility synchronously and return a clear accept or reject.
Commit the refund intent and its outbox event atomically.
Process the provider refund through a queue with an idempotency key.
Publish RefundIssued for ledger and notification consumers.

variants.hint: Idempotency keys belong to the durable-work step.
variants.explanation: Eligibility is the immediate decision; the provider call is durable work; the fact is published afterwards.

variants.title: Build in resilience
variants.context: Retries, timeouts, and dead-letter queues need bounded policies: attempt the smallest durable unit, back off with jitter on transient errors, quarantine exhausted messages with context, then recover deliberately.
variants.prompt: A consumer handles a message that fails intermittently. Put the policy in order.

items.text: Attempt: validate, check the idempotency key, do the smallest durable unit of work.
Back off: retry only recoverable errors with jitter, capped delay, and capped attempts.
Quarantine: move exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue with payload, error, attempts, and correlation context.
Recover: fix the cause, replay deliberately, and verify idempotency protected completed effects.

variants.hint: Quarantine comes after bounded retries, never instead of them.
variants.explanation: Attempt → back off → quarantine → recover. Each control changes load and correctness, so each has a bounded policy.

variants.title: Build in resilience
variants.context: Retries, timeouts, and dead-letter queues need bounded policies: attempt the smallest durable unit, back off with jitter on transient errors, quarantine exhausted messages with context, then recover deliberately.
variants.prompt: A downstream API is throttling. Put the consumer’s behavior in order.

items.text: Process the smallest durable unit and check the idempotency key.
Back off with jitter within a capped retry budget.
After the attempt cap, dead-letter with full context.
An operator repairs, replays, and confirms no duplicate effects.

variants.hint: Throttling is transient; the retry budget still has a cap.
variants.explanation: Bounded backoff protects the dependency; the dead-letter queue protects the rest of the queue.

variants.title: Build in resilience
variants.context: Retries, timeouts, and dead-letter queues need bounded policies: attempt the smallest durable unit, back off with jitter on transient errors, quarantine exhausted messages with context, then recover deliberately.
variants.prompt: A malformed message arrives. Put the correct handling in order.

items.text: Attempt validation; it fails deterministically.
Skip transient backoff, because the error cannot recover on its own.
Quarantine immediately with the payload and error.
Fix the producer or data, then replay under idempotency.

variants.hint: Not every failure deserves a retry.
variants.explanation: Retry only errors that can plausibly recover; permanent failures go straight to quarantine.

variants.title: Separate delivery from effect
variants.context: Delivery and business effect are different facts. A transport promises at-most-once or at-least-once delivery; the application decides whether repeated delivery repeats the operation. An idempotency key lets several attempts converge on one effect.
variants.prompt: A broker redelivers a payment message after a consumer restart. What makes the second delivery harmless?
options: An idempotency key that lets the attempts converge on one durable effect.
optionFeedback: The application, not the transport, decides whether repeated delivery repeats the operation.
At-most-once can lose the payment entirely.
variants.hint: Who decides what a duplicate delivery does?
variants.explanation: At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent effect is how most systems reach one business result.

variants.title: Separate delivery from effect
variants.context: Delivery and business effect are different facts. A transport promises at-most-once or at-least-once delivery; the application decides whether repeated delivery repeats the operation. An idempotency key lets several attempts converge on one effect.
variants.prompt: A sender times out, but the receiver actually completed the operation. What is true?
options: The sender cannot know; a retry needs a stable operation identity to be safe.
optionFeedback: Timeouts are ambiguous across the failure boundary.
The sender only knows the response was lost.
variants.hint: What did the sender actually observe?
variants.explanation: Every remote interaction crosses a failure boundary; design the retry contract for the ambiguous case.

variants.title: Separate delivery from effect
variants.context: Delivery and business effect are different facts. A transport promises at-most-once or at-least-once delivery; the application decides whether repeated delivery repeats the operation. An idempotency key lets several attempts converge on one effect.
variants.prompt: A report takes ten minutes and the caller cannot keep a connection open. Which shape fits?
options: Request-reply with a correlation ID and a later response.
A synchronous call with a ten-minute timeout.
optionFeedback: The request and later response share a correlation ID.
Only the requester needs the result.
variants.hint: How does the reply find its request later?
variants.explanation: Request-reply with correlation suits long-running work the caller cannot wait for.

variants.title: Budget the timeouts
variants.context: Timeouts derive from the end-to-end latency budget; retry budgets stop one failure from multiplying traffic; backoff delays are capped.
variants.prompt: The end-to-end budget is 800 ms. The gateway uses 50 ms and service A uses 200 ms before calling downstream. What remains for the downstream call, including any retries?
variants.hint: Subtract every upstream stage from the budget.
variants.explanation: 800 − 50 − 200 = 550 ms. Derive timeouts from the budget, not a framework default.

mistakes.feedback: Upstream stages already consumed part of the budget.
Both the gateway and service A count.

variants.title: Budget the timeouts
variants.context: Timeouts derive from the end-to-end latency budget; retry budgets stop one failure from multiplying traffic; backoff delays are capped.
variants.prompt: Backoff doubles from 100 ms and is capped at 500 ms. What is the total backoff across four retries?

mistakes.feedback: The fourth delay is capped at 500, not 800.

variants.title: Budget the timeouts
variants.context: Timeouts derive from the end-to-end latency budget; retry budgets stop one failure from multiplying traffic; backoff delays are capped.
variants.prompt: Baseline traffic is 10,000 requests per second and the retry budget allows 20% extra. What is the maximum number of retries per second before retries are shed?
variants.hint: Multiply baseline by the budget percentage.
variants.explanation: 10,000 × 0.2 = 2,000 retries per second. Beyond that, retries multiply the outage instead of surviving it.

mistakes.feedback: That is total traffic; retries alone are 2,000.
